summary: This standards-track memo defines MIB objects for managing the line-code-specific parameters of VDSL interfaces that use multiple carrier modulation. Operators can monitor and configure those lines with SNMP.

plainLanguage.summary: Some fast internet lines over phone wires split the signal into many channels. This document defines the controls and readouts for lines that use this style.

what does power spectral density mean in vdsl mib

subtitle: SNMP objects for the tone, band and power settings of VDSL lines that use multiple carrier modulation.

tldr.problem: The base VDSL MIB manages only the line-code-independent parts of a VDSL line. Lines that use multiple carrier modulation (MCM) also have line-code-specific settings, such as which tones form a band and how much power each tone may use.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4070 defines an optional extension MIB module, VDSL-LINE-EXT-MCM-MIB, with six tables of configuration profile data. Each table is indexed by the profile name from the base VDSL-LINE-MIB.
tldr.outcome: Operators can create and edit MCM profiles over SNMP. A device that does not use MCM does not need to implement the module, and an MCM device that does implement it must support the whole group.

today: RFC 4070 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of this MCM extension to the VDSL line MIB in RFC 3728.

sections.title: What This MIB Module Is For
sections.content:
RFC 4070 defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) for Very High Speed Digital Subscriber Line (VDSL) interfaces. Specifically, it covers the Line Code Specific parameters of VDSL lines that use Multiple Carrier Modulation (MCM) line coding.

It is an optional extension to the VDSL-LINE-MIB in RFC 3728, which handles the line code independent objects. The definitions are based on VDSL specifications from T1E1, ETSI and ITU, and the DSL Forum management framework was also taken into consideration.

MIB objects are normally reached with the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). The module is written in SMIv2, defined in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.
sections.plainLanguage: There is already a rule book for controlling a fast phone-wire internet line. This is an extra chapter for lines that use the many-channels style.

sections.title: How the Module Fits with the VDSL MIB
sections.content:
The module sits in the MIB tree under MIB-2 transmission. The module identity is vdslExtMCMMIB, assigned transmission value 229.

The base VDSL line table marks a line as MCM through vdslLineCoding. When that object is set to MCM, the profile name vdslLineConfProfileName is used as the index to each of the six MCM tables. The existence of an entry in any of these tables is optional.

The description is firm on one point: these objects MUST NOT be used for lines using Single Carrier Modulation (SCM). If a line that does not use MCM references an entry, the entry has no effect on that line.
sections.plainLanguage: Each line points to a named settings sheet. If the line is not the many-channels kind, it simply ignores the extra pages.

sections.title: The Six Profile Tables
sections.content:
All six tables hang off a configuration profile. The group is called vdslMCMGroup.

  • vdslLineMCMConfProfileTable holds one entry per profile with the transmit window length, counted in samples at the sampling rate for the negotiated value of N. The value ranges from 1 to 255.
  • vdslLineMCMConfProfileTxBandTable and vdslLineMCMConfProfileRxBandTable describe transmit and receive bands. Each band has a number, a start tone index and a stop tone index, all in the range 1 to 4096.
  • vdslLineMCMConfProfileTxPSDTable sets a transmit power spectral density (PSD) mask, one tone per row.
  • vdslLineMCMConfProfileMaxTxPSDTable and vdslLineMCMConfProfileMaxRxPSDTable set the maximum transmit and receive PSD per tone.

A profile can have at most one row in the main table and any number (0..n) of rows in each of the other five.
sections.plainLanguage: The settings sheet has six pages: one for a general setting, two for which channels to send and receive on, and three for how strong the signal on each channel may be.

sections.title: Tones and Power Levels
sections.content:
A tone is one of the carriers of an MCM line, identified by an index. A band is a run of tones from a start index to a stop index.

PSD levels are given in steps of 0.5 dBm/Hz with an offset of -140 dBm/Hz. The object type is an Unsigned32 and its units are "0.5dBm/Hz". For the maximum PSD tables, there must not be multiple rows in a profile with the same tone value.
sections.plainLanguage: Each channel gets a number, and its volume is written as a count of small steps up from a very quiet starting point.

sections.title: Creating, Validating and Persisting Rows
sections.content:
Each table has a RowStatus object. A profile is activated by setting it to active, and the system then validates the profile. No column of a row may be modified while the row is active. Before a row can be set to destroy or notInService, it must first be unreferenced from all associated lines.

Validation has extra rules. For the band tables, each entry must be internally consistent (the stop tone must be greater than the start tone) and externally consistent (entries of one profile must not overlap). For the maximum PSD tables, there must be only one entry per tone for a given profile.

All read-create objects SHOULD be stored persistently, and the RFC lists them. The interface indices are also maintained persistently, and the related VACM data SHOULD be stored persistently as well.
sections.plainLanguage: You write the settings, then flip a switch to turn them on, and the device checks they make sense. Once they are on, you cannot change them without switching them off first.

sections.title: Conformance
sections.content: An MCM based VDSL agent does not have to implement this MIB to comply with RFC 3728. If it does implement the extension, the group vdslMCMGroup is mandatory, so all of its objects MUST be implemented. The compliance statement names the single group vdslLineExtMCMGroup.
sections.plainLanguage: Skipping this extra chapter is fine. If you use it, though, you have to do all of it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All the read-create objects are listed as sensitive, because unprotected SET operations can harm network operations. Write access could let an end user raise their service level or affect other users. Because the Vtur side can reach the link and its embedded operations channel, unfiltered changes by a subscriber could generate enough notifications to overwhelm the management interface or element manager.

Readable objects may also be sensitive. Knowing the physical band parameters could help someone apply intentional interference on the bands in use.

Versions of SNMP before SNMPv3 lacked adequate security. The RFC recommends that implementers consider the SNMPv3 security features, with cryptographic authentication and privacy, and says deploying versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED. Operators must make sure only legitimate principals can GET or SET the objects.
sections.plainLanguage: These settings control how a phone line behaves, so only trusted people should be allowed to change or even peek at them.

sections.title: IANA Assignment
sections.content: IANA assigned the transmission value 229 to VDSL-LINE-EXT-MCM-MIB. This is the only IANA action in the document.
sections.plainLanguage: The number registry gave this module its own spot, number 229.
